source_text: {SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Ah yeah I can't wait to see it!

{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}Update pushed to the Visualize window.{PART_001}Visualize window has gray-scale colors based on {SIG_N052} value.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Hey Carrie,{PART_001}he told us where he updated right off the get-go!
{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}{PLAYER_NAME}'s response of {SIG_N044} was accepted last transmission.{PART_001}It looked sideways,{PART_002}so our dimensions were wrong.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}It did look like it was knocked over.

{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}If we are graphing a {SIG_N052} in 3 dimensions,{PART_001}we use the data as X,{PART_002}Y,{PART_003}then Z,{PART_004}where X is horizontal,{PART_005}Y is vertical,{PART_006}and Z is depth.{PART_007}Now Y and Z are flipped.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}X-Z-Y.{PART_001}So they're sayin' the 2nd parameter is near-and-far,{PART_002}and the 3rd is up-and-down?
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}But why is that ordering their convention?{PART_001}Why would they prioritize depth over verticality?
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Why do we organize our dimensions as X-Y-Z?{PART_001}Why that order?
{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}Because we prioritize our horizontal perception over verticality and depth.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}We see the world in 2-dimensions,{PART_001}which eliminates depth.{PART_002}For us humans,{PART_003}our horizontal movement is our easiest to control.{PART_004}We can run along the ground for long distances;{PART_005}we cannot jump high or burrow low.
{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}Our field of vision is biased for the horizontal axis.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Another good point --{PART_001}We can see much wider than we can tall,{PART_002}since our eyes are at the same vertical but different horizontal.
{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}Depth perception we typically order last.{PART_001}Our two eyes do not help.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}My Granny Beth had one good eye.{PART_001}Couldn't pour coffee if it were to save her life.{PART_002}She'd mis-judge and pour it all on the table.{PART_003}Or worse,{PART_004}the customer.{PART_005}Lost her job at a diner that way...
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Given that the aliens organize depth before verticality,{PART_001}I'd reason the aliens prioritize their depth perception over vertical.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}So let me get this straight:{PART_001}you're sayin' if Granny were an alien,{PART_002}she'd have no issue pouring coffee?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Um.{PART_001}That might be an oddly succint way to put it actually.{PART_002}But the question remains?{PART_003}Why do they prioritize depth perception over vertical perception?{PART_004}What biology would that entail?{PART_005}What sensory organs do they possess?{PART_006}What world did they evolve to perceive?
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Carrie,{PART_001}I'm unconvinced.{PART_002}Their scientific progress has us beat.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}There's no doubt about that.{PART_001}They sent the meteor--{PART_002}we haven't.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}The meteor itself is a marvel of engineering,{PART_001}both in dealing with how you launch that kind of mass out of orbit,{PART_002}then accelerate it to the ridiculous speed that they did.{PART_003}And here's the kicker:{PART_004}I did the math.{PART_005}If the meteor continued at the interstellar speed they told us,{PART_006}then on impact,{PART_007}it would've done some serious damage to the planet.{PART_008}The meteor somehow detected the little blue Earth it approached,{PART_009}and decelerated to avoid wiping out any potential,{PART_010}fragile life.{PART_011}Tell me,{PART_012}are we capable of ANY of that?
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Well I was!{PART_001}Kinda.{PART_002}And the answer is no,{PART_003}we can't do that.{PART_004}It's far beyond us.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Consider what we know now that we didn't know just 70 years ago.{PART_001}I'm still not convinced this isn't that different from our current technology.{PART_002}We just sent men to the moon.{PART_003}Give it another 70 years and we could launch smart meteors too.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}70 years ago is the turn of the century...{PART_001}I guess that's when Einstein got around to relativity.{PART_002}I reckon by 2040,{PART_003}launching meteors or satellites into deep space could be tenable.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}And if that's the case,{PART_001}we're back to the original question:{PART_002}Why are the aliens similar in their scientific progress?{PART_003}Why are we potentially 70 years away?{PART_004}That's merely a single human lifetime.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}I'm still thinking about the alien technology,{PART_001}Carrie.{PART_002}You have a point.{PART_003}Though I'm ashamed to say we're still pretty far behind them...{PART_004}I don't know if 70 years will be enough to catch up.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}I have a theory why we're not so different.{PART_001}What would've happened had we received the meteor 10,000 years ago?
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}We wouldn't have noticed.{PART_001}It's the geoseismic stations that heard it land.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Right.{PART_001}And maybe some ancient humans would've stumbled upon the crater in Alaska.{PART_002}Maybe they would've made it a worship site.{PART_003}But there's no chance they're detecting the radio wave transmissions.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}The message would fall on deaf ears.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Only at this point,{PART_001}only when you reach our current level of human technology,{PART_002}will a civilization recognize similar levels of technology.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}This hypothetical prehistoric alien meteor,{PART_001}wouldn't we modern day humans discover it?

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}If it were still intact,{PART_001}not eroded,{PART_002}not destroyed,{PART_003}still functional.{PART_004}I mean,{PART_005}there must be a battery inside to power these transmissions.{PART_006}What if it died?{PART_007}There are a million things that time can do to break things down.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Your idea makes sense.{PART_001}Only with modern technology would we even recognize the message.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}It's sad to think of the implications,{PART_001}the possibility of previous messages left undiscovered.{PART_002}Civilizations that were never heard,{PART_003}despite their efforts.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}My own argument troubles me.{PART_001}The technological intersection,{PART_002}I don't know.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Requiring advanced science to detect advanced messages?{PART_001}It's troubling to imagine those civilizations unheard...

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}It's not just the civilizations unheard,{PART_001}the messages missed.{PART_002}There's another frightening implication.{PART_003}If humans are only seeing this message now because we have the technology to recognize it,{PART_004}then it's possible there are other interstellar mediums that we're not advanced enough to detect.{PART_005}Maybe we are the prehistoric humans,{PART_006}unaware of the extraterrestrial meteor.{PART_007}This meteor is just a  primitive enough message that we could see it.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}What if other aliens are tapping some thread of the universe that we have not yet found?{PART_001}What if we are in the dark,{PART_002}unaware of the sea of information that the highly advanced are sending?{PART_003}Aliens tappin' morse code on quantum wire.{PART_004}I'm talkin' faster than light communication.{PART_005}What if we're the only ones unaware?
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Carrie,{PART_001}I'm gettin' far too ahead of myself.{PART_002}I'm stressin' over nothin'.{PART_003}Well it's not nothin',{PART_004}but it's needless and perhaps misinformed.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}You ever hear of the Drake Equation?

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}It's a formula,{PART_001}made about 10 years ago,{PART_002}that calculates the probability of the existence of other intelligent life.{PART_003}It factors in the amount of stars,{PART_004}the average number of planets per star,{PART_005}the average proportion of planets that can host life,{PART_006}the average rate at which said life becomes intelligent,{PART_007}and a handful of other variables,{PART_008}the whole kit and kaboodle.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}We've got no idea.{PART_001}And that's my point.{PART_002}We don't know any of the variables.{PART_003}We haven't a clue how many stars there are,{PART_004}how many planets they average,{PART_005}how many host life,{PART_006}how often life becomes intelligent.{PART_007}We haven't a clue.{PART_008}The entire probability space is beyond us.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Exactly.{PART_001}We're so concerned that there could have been other messages,{PART_002}or that there still are now,{PART_003}faster than light.{PART_004}I'm confident in Einstein's theories,{PART_005}no information can exceed the speed of light.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}There may have been previous messages we missed,{PART_001}but I reckon it's unlikely.{PART_002}The truth is,{PART_003}we needed modern technology to detect the meteor,{PART_004}to interface with the transmissions,{PART_005}and to understand its contents.{PART_006}We have the science to handle their message and for that I'm grateful.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}And I imagine the aliens would be too.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Maybe it's merely coincidence...{PART_001}that at the dawn of humanity's endeavor to space,{PART_002}merely decades after we've first peered into the atom,{PART_003}and a century into sending radio waves,{PART_004}are we the recipient of an interstellar message that demands all of said knowledge.{PART_005}But if it is merely coincidence,{PART_006}it is one for which I will remain forever grateful.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Jokes aside,{PART_001}does it strike anyone peculiar,{PART_002}that the aliens don't know everything?
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}What,{PART_001}in order to send an interstellar message,{PART_002}ya gotta know everything?!{PART_003}That's quite a high bar, Carrie!
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I find it odd that their level of scientific progress is similar to ours.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}They've synthesized {SIG_N055}'s as large as,{PART_001}what was it,{PART_002}{SIG_N056} 210?{PART_003}One {SIG_N056} with 210 {SIG_N060}'s!?{PART_004}Are ya kidding me?!

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Some sure.{PART_001}But 210 is a whole 'nother scale.{PART_002}We didn't even know that {SIG_N055}'s beyond 137 would be possible!{PART_003}It's theorized that at that point,{PART_004}the electrostatic repulsion in the nucleus overcomes the strong nuclear force!{PART_005}Humanity is nowhere near that!

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I'm nowhere near understanding that...{PART_001}But still,{PART_002}they're not orders of magnitude more advanced than us.{PART_003}The fact that we as humans can make that claim,{PART_004}and that you can follow along to that level,{PART_005}shows we are somewhat close.{PART_006}It's comparable at least.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}In the Reference Tab,{PART_001}$animA3he calculated the conversions for all of the alien units.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}$animC4Bautista,{PART_001}I would normally continue admonishing you about your poor attention to sleep.{PART_002}$animC2But selfishly,{PART_003}I'm glad you worked on this update.{PART_004}$animC5That prior stretch of transmissions,{PART_005}I had very little input.{PART_006}I could hardly follow along.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Carrie,{PART_001}I don't think I've had the chance to ask you this.{PART_002}Why linguistics?{PART_003}Why are you a linguist?{PART_004}What hooked you?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I earned my Bachelor's of Science degree in Linguistics from the University of Massachusetts.{PART_001}I completed my PhD there as well before I was hired as an assistant professor at Boston College.{PART_002}I became a professor and achieved tenure at the age of 33,{PART_003}the youngest woman at the school to do so.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}That's great and all…{PART_001}but I asked ya 'why?'{PART_002}What drew you to linguistics?{PART_003}I mean you're certainly good at it!{PART_004}I wanna know what drove you into the field.{PART_005}I'm curious is all.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I appreciate learning new languages and studying now meaning is derived from words.{PART_001}I find I understand the world better when I put communication itself under a microscope.{PART_002}It's deeply fascinating and introspective.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Ya know Carrie,{PART_001}that still wasn't an answer.{PART_002}Your whole spiel about language and microscopes and stuff,{PART_003}it was cool but,{PART_004}still not an answer.{PART_005}I could've read that answer in a college brochure.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Well it's my answer.{PART_001}Sorry you don't like it.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}We've been working side-by-side on this project almost every day for nearly 5 months.{PART_001}Heaven forbid I want to get to know you…

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}My dad was in the airforce.{PART_001}We moved every 2 years.{PART_002}We bounced around all over the nation and the post-war globe.{PART_003}We lived in Spain,{PART_004}we lived in Sweden,{PART_005}and we lived in Japan.{PART_006}I was frequently exposed to new languages and I grew a liking to them.{PART_007}Does that answer suffice?
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}And you're dodgy!{PART_001}Though I appreciate you for sharing that much.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Well it's all the answer you'll receive.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Fine.{PART_001}The people were nice.{PART_002}Winters were cold.{PART_003}I thought once we moved back to the United States afterwards,{PART_004}we would not move again.{PART_005}My father broke his promise and we moved to Japan.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}So I'm guessin' Japan wasn't very fun for you?
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}No.{PART_001}Quite the contrary.{PART_002}My two years in Japan were some of the most profound years of my upbringing.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I was 16,{PART_001}didn't want to be there,{PART_002}mad at my father for moving us yet again.{PART_003}I wanted to hole myself in my room and stuff my nose in books.{PART_004}I thought if I stuck it out those two years until I graduated,{PART_005}no one would be hurt.{PART_006}I wouldn't be hurt.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}That doesn't sound very profound…{PART_001}I guess they were good books!
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}No,{PART_001}that part was not.{PART_002}But it didn't last long.{PART_003}The books got stale,{PART_004}and I started wandering off-base.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}My dad was stationed at the Misawa Air Base.{PART_001}It was a small,{PART_002}located in Northern Japan,{PART_003}and recently converted to an American base.{PART_004}It was just two years removed from the Korean Conflict,{PART_005}so amenities were minimal.{PART_006}No shopping mall,{PART_007}no movie theater,{PART_008}hardly a park.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}There was a playground,{PART_001}but I was 16.{PART_002}All I had was the school.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}You see why I began to wander off base.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Carrie,{PART_001}the other day you were telling me about life stationed in Japan.{PART_002}You mentioned wandering off base.{PART_003}What'd you do?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I found this fishing marina,{PART_001}a short hike down to the water.{PART_002}I'd watch the boats come in,{PART_003}rolling with the sea fog that rolled in with dusk.{PART_004}While docking,{PART_005}the fishermen were automatic,{PART_006}rarely instructional or even speaking.{PART_007}They were focused and synchronized.{PART_008}Only after stepping off the pier did they begin to talk,{PART_009}mostly in deep,{PART_010}husky grunts.{PART_011}I remember that bizarre feeling,{PART_012}the perplexation at how such amorphous,{PART_013}hasty chirps of sound could have meant something to each other.{PART_014}I'd watch the body language,{PART_015}often strangely reminiscent of Swedes.{PART_016}The arms pinned to the sides,{PART_017}the nodding of the heads that brought the whole neck down with it.{PART_018}Bows were rare here,{PART_019}rarer than what I had learned in school,{PART_020}though that was more from rumor than curriculum.{PART_021}But deep nodding was common,{PART_022}usually accompanied with a brief but affirmative "eh" or "hi".{PART_023}Though I noticed,{PART_024}"hi" wasn't a greeting.{PART_025}It seemed to mean "yes."
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}You were sayin',{PART_001}about the guys workin' the marina?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}The fishermen!{PART_001}I wanted to hear them better,{PART_002}so one evening, I moved closer to the dock down at the water.{PART_003}And that's when I heard a sweet voice behind me.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I have no idea.{PART_001}I couldn't understand any of it.{PART_002}It was all in Japanese.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Hadn't you been living in Japan?{PART_001}How'd you not pick up any of the language?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}We lived on base,{PART_001}major difference.{PART_002}It's American soil with American people and American businesses.{PART_003}Anyways,{PART_004}I turned to face the voice,{PART_005}and I saw her.{PART_006}She was a bit more surprised to see me than I was she.{PART_007}She tried to hide her surprise,{PART_008}but failed.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I wasn't sure at first.{PART_001}Neither of us were.{PART_002}We stared at each other for a few seconds,{PART_003}both clearly wanting to greet each other,{PART_004}but we were unsure how to get it across.{PART_005}I was suddenly quite proud.{PART_006}I knew what to say.{PART_007}I waved and said "Ohio",{PART_008}something I had heard from the fishermen when I visited in the mornings.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I have since learned it meant "good morning",{PART_001}though it was evening when I said it to Nozomi.{PART_002}You could imagine the look on her face.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}She had sat down on the bench beside me.{PART_001}She asked me a question,{PART_002}though I hadn't a clue what she said.{PART_003}I paused and thought.{PART_004}She wanted to have a conversation.{PART_005}And when you start a conversation with a stranger—{PART_006}I figured it out!
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}So how'd your little conversation with Nozomi go?
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Hah.{PART_001}You say it just like how I did that day.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Diphthongs.{PART_001}You're morphing your vowels.{PART_002}The o's in Nozomi aren't like English o's.{PART_003}We make two vowel sounds: "oh" and "oo".{PART_004}They blend together quickly as "oh-oo".

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}When Nozomi and I exchanged names,{PART_001}she complimented mine.{PART_002}I could tell,{PART_003}something about facial expressions,{PART_004}her voice's pitch.{PART_005}But I was able to figure out her sentence without understanding any of the words.{PART_006}Weird.{PART_007}I say I didn't understand it,{PART_008}but I did.{PART_009}I couldn't break it apart into words,{PART_010}sure,{PART_011}but I could tell you what it meant.{PART_012}How's that different from understanding?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Again,{PART_001}I tried to speak Japanese.{PART_002}I wanted to impress her.{PART_003}"Kowaiyo!" I tried complimenting like she did.{PART_004}She smiled that same sweet smile,{PART_005}but again,{PART_006}I could tell it wasn't quite right.{PART_007}She wasn't good at hiding her emotions,{PART_008}though she tried.{PART_009}I appreciated the feedback more than she realized,{PART_010}so I appreciated her inability to hide her emotions.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}So did you and Nozomi ever see each other again?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Haha,{PART_001}certainly.{PART_002}We started meeting every day after school.{PART_003}Over the next year, I learned about her,{PART_004}about Japan, and an awful about the Japanese language.{PART_005}It was our primary medium.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}I taught her some,{PART_001}because she was curious and I was excited to share.{PART_002}But it largely made more sense to use Japanese.{PART_003}We were in Japan.{PART_004}Unless I brought something off base,{PART_005}everything we had was written or printed in Japanese.{PART_006}When in Rome,{PART_007}do as the Romans.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Why was Nozomi always at the pier?{PART_001}Was she a wandering weirdo like you?

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Her dad worked at the pier.{PART_001}He was a fisherman.{PART_002}They had always lived here.{PART_003}We were only here because of my father's assignment.{PART_004}She frowned when I first said told her he was in the airforce,{PART_005}but she tried to hide it.{PART_006}I learned it wasn't anything personal.{PART_007}Her family was sad to see the Misawa air base converted to an American base.{PART_008}And though that first began about a decade prior with the end of the second world war,{PART_009}I could understand the lingering discomfort.{PART_010}They weren't threatened,{PART_011}but it was a painful reminder of their nation's defeat,{PART_012}and perhaps more dreadful,{PART_013}a dark stain on their nation as a whole.

{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Nozomi and I were the same age,{PART_001}born during the war,{PART_002}but too young to remember much.{PART_003}It was perhaps a rather fortunate time to be born,{PART_004}just after the great depression,{PART_005}and with the world's worst conflict not yet comprehensible for either of us.{PART_006}We came out on the other side of it,{PART_007}something strange that we could share,{PART_008}despite the antagonism our recently warring nations shared.
